outline.description: Introduces the problem of few-shot tabular learning, limitations of existing LLM-based approaches, and the core idea and contributions of FeatLLM: using LLMs as feature engineers to extract rule-based features that enable simple, cheap, and scalable inference.
subtopics: Why few-shot learning on tabular data matters in real-world applications
Challenges with end-to-end LLM inference: per-sample cost, fine-tuning constraints, and prompt length limits
FeatLLM at a glance: LLM-driven rule extraction, binary feature generation, simple downstream modeling
Key benefits: API-only access, no LLM fine-tuning, reduced inference latency, prompt-size scalability via bagging
Summary of results: robust performance across 13 datasets, ~10% average improvement over TabLLM/STUNT

outline.chapter_title: Background: Tabular ML, Few-Shot Learning, and Language-Interfaced Methods
outline.description: Provides foundational concepts and prior work that inform FeatLLM, including classical tabular ML, few-shot strategies, and LLM-based tabular approaches.
subtopics: Classical baselines: Logistic Regression, XGBoost, Random Forest
Few-shot learning in tabular data: semi/unsupervised pretraining, transfer learning, synthetic priors (e.g., TabPFN)
Limitations of augmentations for heterogeneous tabular features
Language-interfaced tabular learning: data serialization, prompts, in-context learning vs parameter-efficient tuning
Representative methods: In-context prompting, TABLET, TabLLM; their pros/cons in low-shot settings

outline.description: Defines the tabular classification setting, notation for features and labels, and the few-shot regime targeted by FeatLLM.
subtopics: Dataset notation: N labeled samples, d features, class labels
Feature names and natural language definitions
k-shot training subset selection
Binary and multi-class classification scope
Evaluation metrics overview (AUC/AUROC focus)

outline.description: Presents the full pipeline of FeatLLM from prompts to predictions, including rule extraction, feature generation, simple modeling, and ensembling.
subtopics: Two-stage use of LLMs: (1) rule extraction; (2) rule parsing into executable code
Binary feature construction per class from rule satisfaction
Lightweight downstream model for class likelihoods
Repeat-and-ensemble strategy with bagging for robustness and scalability
Design principles: interpretability, low inference cost, practicality with API-only models

outline.description: Details the prompt design that guides LLMs to discover high-quality, class-discriminative rules using both prior knowledge and few-shot examples.
subtopics: Basic information section: task description, label schema, feature descriptions and types, serialized few-shot examples
Serialization format for examples: “f1 is x1. ... fd is xd. Answer: y”
Reasoning instructions: two-step process separating prior knowledge reasoning from example-based deduction
Response instructions: strict output formats, type-aware rule templates, fixed number of rules per class (e.g., 10)
Avoiding spurious rules: focusing attention, constraining logic, leveraging feature types

outline.chapter_title: From Natural Language Rules to Executable Features
outline.description: Explains how natural language rules are reliably parsed into executable code to generate binary feature matrices, leveraging LLMs’ code understanding.
subtopics: Challenges of parsing free-form text: syntactic variability and normalization
LLM-assisted code generation: function specs, inputs/outputs, and rule text as context
Execution flow: generating Python code, safe execution considerations, and data type handling
Creating per-class binary features indicating rule satisfaction
Quality control: formatting constraints, schema validation, type checks

outline.chapter_title: Estimating Class Likelihood with Simple, Constrained Models
outline.description: Covers the downstream modeling that learns the importance of rule-derived features using a linear model with non-negative weights and softmax outputs.
subtopics: Feature vector per class: z_k ∈ {0,1}^R from R rules
Linear model without bias; weight vector w_k and positivity projection (max(w_k, 0))
Softmax over class logits; cross-entropy training objective
Why non-negativity: ensuring rules don’t decrease class likelihoods
Training protocol: Adam optimizer, learning rate 0.01, 200 epochs, k-fold cross-validation for early stopping

outline.chapter_title: Ensembling and Bagging for Robustness and Prompt Scalability
outline.description: Describes how FeatLLM increases reliability and handles prompt length constraints using ensembling, temperature, demo order shuffling, and bagging.
subtopics: Multiple trials (ensembles): averaging class probabilities over T rule sets
Injecting diversity: higher temperature and randomizing demonstration order
Instance and feature bagging to reduce prompt size and encourage complementary rules
Self-consistency rationale: frequently rediscovered rules are more reliable
Trade-offs: ensemble size vs performance gains; diminishing returns around ~20 ensembles

outline.description: Outlines datasets, baselines, and implementation details used to evaluate FeatLLM in low-shot regimes.
subtopics: Datasets (13): Adult, Bank, Blood, Car, Communities, Credit-g, Diabetes, Heart, Myocardial, Cultivars, NHANES, Sequence-type, Solution-mix
Dataset diversity: recent UCI additions and synthetic sets to avoid LLM memorization
Baselines (9): LogReg, XGBoost, RandomForest, SCARF, STUNT, TabPFN, In-context, TABLET, TabLLM
LLM backbone and settings: GPT-3.5 API use, temperature 0.5, top-p default; 10 rules/class; 20 ensembles
Training details: linear model optimization; fair replication of baselines; cross-validation and grid search for classical ML

outline.description: Summarizes performance outcomes, efficiency comparisons, and strengths of FeatLLM across diverse datasets and operating conditions.
subtopics: Overall performance: FeatLLM top-1 or top-2 across datasets; strong gains in 4-shot settings vs 32-shot classical ML
Scalability: success on high-dimensional datasets where other LLM methods struggle with context limits
Training and inference time: low inference latency comparable to classical methods; far cheaper than per-sample LLM calls
Ablation study: effects of removing tuning, ensembling, feature descriptions, and reasoning step
Hyperparameter sensitivity: ensembles and rules-per-class trade-offs; convergence around 20 ensembles and ~10 rules

outline.description: Investigates the informativeness of rule-based features, resistance to spurious correlations, and why FeatLLM remains robust in few-shot regimes.
subtopics: Feature informativeness: AUROC of rule-features vs labels; proportion exceeding 0.5 before and after weight tuning
Automatic pruning: low-utility rules down-weighted during training
Spurious correlation stress test: adding irrelevant columns and measuring degradation
Why robustness emerges: prior-knowledge-first reasoning and type-aware rule extraction
Caveats: vulnerability when attached columns are closely related to the task

outline.chapter_title: Practical Guidance, Limitations, and Future Directions
outline.description: Provides actionable instructions for deploying FeatLLM, discusses limitations and ethical considerations, and outlines extensions and research opportunities.
subtopics: Applying FeatLLM step-by-step: data preparation, feature descriptions, prompt crafting, selecting shots
Managing prompt size: instance/feature bagging, curating demonstrations, balancing rules per class
Cost and runtime planning: batching API calls, parallelization, ensemble sizing
Failure modes and troubleshooting: parsing mismatches, type errors, overly broad or redundant rules
Limitations: reliance on LLM prior knowledge and potential biases, prompt sensitivity, low-shot focus
Ethical and broader impacts: domain biases, misinformation risks, high-stakes domains (finance/healthcare)
Extensions: alternative LLM backbones, richer rule grammars, regression tasks, calibration, integration with AutoML, interpretability tooling
Key takeaways and when to use FeatLLM in practice
